items.topic: Home oxygen safety — no smoking; keep away from open flame/heat; avoid petroleum-based lotions
items.stem: The nurse teaches a client starting home oxygen therapy. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Do not smoke or allow smoking near oxygen; keep oxygen away from open flames/heat sources; avoid petroleum-based lotions on the face or upper body
Smoking is safe if the oxygen flow is turned down to 1 L/min
Petroleum jelly is preferred on the nose and face while oxygen is in use
Place oxygen equipment next to a wood stove to warm the gas before use

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus: no smoking where oxygen is used; keep oxygen about 6 feet from heat; avoid Vaseline/petroleum creams unless advised. COPD Foundation: do not smoke; keep equipment 5–10 feet from open flames; avoid oil/petroleum-based products on face/upper chest.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Smoking near oxygen is prohibited regardless of flow rate.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Petroleum-based products are discouraged; water-based preferred.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Keep oxygen away from open flames/heat.

items.topic: NGN matrix — home oxygen fire-safety teaching actions
items.stem: For a client prescribed continuous home oxygen, indicate whether each teaching point is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Post and enforce a no-smoking rule wherever oxygen is used
Keep oxygen equipment several feet away from open flames and heat sources (e.g., stove, fireplace, candles)
Apply petroleum jelly liberally to the nares and face while oxygen is running
Encourage visitors to smoke in the same room if the window is open

rationales.R2: Indicated. Keep oxygen away from open flames/heat (≈6 ft MedlinePlus; 5–10 ft COPD Foundation).
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Avoid petroleum-based lotions on face/upper body.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Smoking near oxygen is prohibited.

items.topic: Postoperative DVT prevention — early ambulation / prevent immobility
items.stem: Which nursing action best supports prevention of postoperative deep vein thrombosis related to mobility?

options.text: Promote early ambulation and limit prolonged immobility as the client’s condition allows
Keep the client on strict bed rest for several days even when medically cleared to walk
Discourage all leg movement so the surgical incision can rest completely
Massage the calves vigorously every hour to break up clots

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: early mobilization/ambulation supports thromboprophylaxis. Merck: preventive measures include ambulation and prevention of immobility.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Prolonged immobility increases DVT risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Vigorous calf massage is not evidence-based prevention.

items.topic: Rubella — Droplet Precautions until 7 days after rash onset
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A school-age client is admitted with confirmed rubella (German measles). Which isolation plan is appropriate?

options.text: Droplet Precautions until 7 days after the onset of the rash
Airborne Precautions only until the fever resolves
Standard Precautions alone with no transmission-based isolation
Contact Precautions for 24 hours after starting antibiotics

items.topic: Disseminated herpes zoster — Airborne + Contact Precautions
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: An older adult is admitted with disseminated herpes zoster (shingles with lesions outside the primary dermatomes). Which precautions are required?

options.text: Airborne and Contact Precautions (with Standard Precautions) for the duration of illness / until lesions are dry and crusted
Droplet Precautions only for 24 hours after starting antivirals
Standard Precautions alone with lesions left uncovered in a shared room
Contact Precautions without airborne isolation for disseminated disease

rationales.A: Correct. CDC Appendix A: disseminated zoster — Airborne + Contact + Standard for duration of illness. CDC shingles IC: disseminated — Airborne and Contact until lesions dry and scabbed.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Requires Airborne + Contact, not Droplet-only.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Airborne also required when disseminated.

items.topic: Insulin injection — rotate sites; avoid repeated use of lumpy sites
items.stem: The nurse teaches a client who self-injects insulin subcutaneously. Which teaching point is correct?

options.text: Rotate injection sites and avoid repeatedly using the same spot, especially areas that are lumpy, firm, or numb
Always inject into the exact same abdominal spot for consistent absorption
Inject only into bruised areas so healing tissue absorbs insulin faster
Shake NPH insulin vigorously until foamy before every dose

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: rotate sites to prevent fatty deposits and site irritation. MedlinePlus: keep a chart so you do not inject the same place all the time; avoid lumpy, firm, or numb spots.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Repeated same-site use risks lipohypertrophy/poor absorption.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Cloudy insulin is rolled, not shaken vigorously (OpenStax/MedlinePlus teaching).

items.topic: IV infiltration — cool swollen site; stop infusion and remove catheter
items.stem: A peripheral IV site is swollen and cool to the touch, and the client reports pain at the site. What is the priority nursing action?

options.text: Stop the infusion and remove the IV catheter per protocol, then restart access at another site if still needed
Increase the infusion rate to clear the swelling
Ignore the findings if the pump is not alarming
Flush forcefully with 20 mL of undiluted potassium chloride

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: infiltration causes pain, swelling, cool skin; stop IV fluids immediately and remove the IV. NCBI Open RN: discontinue the site and relocate the IV per policy.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Increasing rate worsens tissue fluid extravasation.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Clinical signs require action even without pump alarms.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Dangerous and unrelated; do not force flush into an infiltrated site.

items.topic: IV phlebitis — redness and tenderness along the vein; stop and remove catheter
items.stem: Which finding best suggests phlebitis at a peripheral IV site, requiring the nurse to stop the infusion and remove the catheter?

options.text: Redness and tenderness along the path of the vein
A cool, pale swollen area without vein inflammation signs
A dry intact dressing with no client discomfort
Blood return present with a soft, nontender site

items.topic: Acute mania — calm clear communication; do not challenge grandiosity; prioritize safety
items.stem: A client in acute mania is agitated, speaking rapidly, and making grandiose plans to leave against advice. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Use a calm demeanor, give concise clear directions, avoid arguing about grandiose ideas, and prioritize a safe environment
Loudly debate each grandiose claim until the client admits they are false
Encourage a large stimulating group activity to burn off energy
Leave the client unsupervised in a crowded waiting area

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: during manic phases maintain a calm demeanor, provide concise clear directions, avoid challenging grandiosity, and ensure a safe environment. Merck: manic episodes involve severe impairment/risky behavior that may require hospitalization — safety is priority.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Challenging grandiosity can escalate agitation.
rationales.C: Incorrect. High stimulation is counterproductive in acute mania.

items.topic: NGN bowtie — acute dystonia from antipsychotic: recognize and treat with benztropine/diphenhydramine
items.stem: A client who recently started a first-generation antipsychotic develops sudden torticollis and tongue spasms. Complete the bowtie: most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.

conditions.text: Tardive dyskinesia only (late irreversible choreiform movements)

actions.text: Notify the provider and administer benztropine or diphenhydramine as ordered (IV/IM)
Hold further doses of the causative antipsychotic pending provider guidance
Encourage the client to ignore the spasms and continue the same antipsychotic dose without assessment
Start a high-dose SSRI immediately as first-line therapy for the spasms
Force oral intake of a large high-carbohydrate meal as the only intervention

parameters.text: Airway patency and ability to swallow/speak (watch for laryngeal involvement)
Resolution of muscle spasms / dystonic movements after treatment
Peak expiratory flow only as the sole monitoring plan
Urine specific gravity every minute without neuromuscular assessment
Orthostatic blood pressure after sprint exercise only

rationales.K1: Incorrect. Tardive dyskinesia is a late effect, not the acute spasmodic torticollis/tongue spasm picture.
rationales.K2: Correct. OpenStax: dystonia includes spasms of tongue, back, legs, neck — an EPS of antipsychotics. Merck: acute dystonic reactions (e.g., torticollis, oculogyric crisis).
rationales.K3: Incorrect. Serotonin syndrome is a different toxidrome.
rationales.A1: Correct. Merck: treat acute dystonia with benztropine IV/IM or diphenhydramine IV/IM.
rationales.A2: Correct. OpenStax/Merck: monitor EPS so treatment can be given and antipsychotic regimen adjusted/changed.
rationales.A3: Incorrect. Acute dystonia requires prompt treatment.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. SSRIs are not treatment for dystonia.
rationales.P1: Correct. Merck notes laryngeal dystonia may threaten airway.
rationales.P2: Correct. Reassess spasm resolution after anticholinergic/antihistamine therapy.
rationales.P3: Incorrect. Peak flow alone misses airway/neuromuscular priorities.
rationales.P5: Incorrect. Not priority monitoring for acute dystonia.

items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Consent practice guideline under Ontario HCCA: capacity assessed relative to a specific treatment.
items.topic: Ontario consent — capacity is treatment-specific; capable client decides
items.stem: An Ontario nurse reviews consent for two different procedures proposed for the same client. Which statement reflects CNO/HCCA capacity principles?

options.text: Capacity is treatment-specific — a client may be capable for one treatment and incapable for another; if capable, the client decides
Once found incapable for any decision, the client is permanently incapable for all future treatments
Nurses may independently override a capable client’s refusal whenever the nurse disagrees
A family member may consent for a clearly capable adult who refuses treatment

rationales.A: Correct. CNO Consent: capacity relates to a specific treatment; a person could be capable for one treatment and incapable for another; if the client is capable, the client makes the decision.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Capacity is decision/treatment-specific and can change.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Practitioners lack authority to decide for capable clients except limited emergencies.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Capable clients decide for themselves; SDM is used when the client is incapable.
